title: Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS)
subtitle: How a network access server asks one central database whether to let a user in, and on what terms.
summary: RADIUS lets a Network Access Server, such as a dial-up modem pool, hand a user's credentials to a central server and act on the answer. One UDP request asks "may this user in?", and the reply says yes or no and carries the settings the user's session should get. The password is hidden with a keyed MD5 scheme and replies are authenticated with a shared secret. This 2000 revision obsoletes RFC 2138, and the protocol it describes is still how much network access is controlled today.

eli5.summary: A door guard does not keep the list of who may come in. Each time someone knocks, the guard phones the main office, asks "is this person allowed?", and does whatever the office says, including which rooms the visitor may use.

questions: why does radius use udp instead of tcp
how does radius hide the user password
what is a network access server
what is the difference between access-accept and access-reject

tldr.problem: Every dial-up server keeping its own user list is hard to manage and hard to secure.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Access Server sends an Access-Request over UDP to a central RADIUS server, which answers Access-Accept, Access-Reject or Access-Challenge, with attributes describing the service to deliver. A shared secret hides the password and signs the reply.
tldr.outcome: One user database can serve many access devices, and the same design still underpins Wi-Fi, VPN and switch-port logins, though its MD5-based protection is now considered weak.

today: RADIUS is still one of the most widely deployed ways to control network access. Enterprise Wi-Fi (802.1X), VPN gateways, switches and ISP broadband systems commonly ask a RADIUS server whether a user may connect. Well-known servers include FreeRADIUS, and Microsoft's Network Policy Server speaks the protocol too. The core packet format here is unchanged, but later RFCs patched and extended it, including RFC 5080 and RFC 6929. In practice RADIUS traffic is often wrapped in extra protection such as IPsec or TLS.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2865 describes a protocol for carrying authentication, authorization and configuration information between a Network Access Server (NAS) that wants to authenticate its links and a shared authentication server. It obsoletes RFC 2138, and a change log at the end lists what moved.

The RFC names four key features. It is client/server: the NAS is the client, and the server decides. It provides network security through a shared secret that is never sent over the network, plus encrypted user passwords. It allows flexible authentication, including PPP PAP or CHAP and UNIX login. And it is extensible, because every transaction is made of variable-length Attribute-Length-Value triples, so new attributes do not disturb existing implementations.

The RFC says that the RADIUS server can itself act as a proxy client to other RADIUS servers or other kinds of authentication servers. That is how roaming between providers works.
sections.eli5: Instead of every door guard keeping their own guest list, they all phone one office. The office keeps the one true list and says yes or no, and also what the guest is allowed to do.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The RFC opens with a management problem. Managing dispersed serial line and modem pools for large numbers of users "can create the need for significant administrative support". Since modem pools are by definition a link to the outside world, they need careful attention to security, authorization and accounting.

The answer is to manage a single "database" of users. It supports authentication (verifying user name and password) and also holds the configuration information that says what kind of service to deliver, for example SLIP, PPP, telnet or rlogin. Every NAS then asks the same server instead of carrying its own copy.

The table compares this with keeping accounts on each device.
sections.eli5: If every guard has a separate list, you must update every list when someone joins or leaves. With one list, you change it once.

sections.title: Operation
sections.content:
When a user connects, the client collects credentials, either from a login prompt or from PPP authentication packets. It builds an Access-Request carrying attributes such as the user's name, the hidden password, the client's ID and the port the user is on. The request goes to the server over the network. If no response comes back in time the client re-sends it, and it may fall back to an alternate server. The RFC leaves the retry and fallback algorithms unspecified.

The server must first recognise the client: a request from a client with no shared secret "MUST be silently discarded". Then it looks up the user and checks every requirement. If something fails it replies Access-Reject. If it wants more proof, such as a one-time code, it replies Access-Challenge, and the client prompts the user and sends a new Access-Request with a new ID that includes the State attribute from the challenge. If everything passes it replies Access-Accept with the configuration for the service, for example the IP address, MTU and compression to use for PPP.

The RFC says keep-alive probes are "strongly discouraged" because they add load and give no useful information. If you want to monitor the server, it says to use SNMP.
sections.eli5: The guard sends the visitor's name and password to the office. The office answers "yes, here are the rules", "no", or "first, ask them this secret question".

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
Exactly one RADIUS packet is carried in the data field of one UDP datagram, with destination port 1812. Early deployments used port 1645, which conflicts with the "datametrics" service, so 1812 is the officially assigned number. Replies swap source and destination ports.

The header is four fields. Code (1 octet) gives the packet type: 1 Access-Request, 2 Access-Accept, 3 Access-Reject, 4 Accounting-Request, 5 Accounting-Response, 11 Access-Challenge, with 12 and 13 reserved (Status-Server and Status-Client, experimental) and 255 reserved. Identifier (1 octet) matches requests with replies. Length (2 octets) covers the whole packet; the minimum is 20 and the maximum is 4096, and anything beyond Length is treated as padding. The Authenticator is 16 octets. Everything after the 20-byte header is a list of attributes.

Each attribute is Type (1 octet), Length (1 octet, counting Type and Length) and a Value. Text values are UTF-8 and are 1 to 253 octets; zero-length values must not be sent.
sections.eli5: Every message is a short form with a type stamp, a number to match it to its question, a length, and a scrambled signature, followed by as many labelled notes as needed.

sections.title: Authenticators and Password Hiding
sections.content:
The Authenticator field does two jobs. In an Access-Request it is a 16-octet random number, the Request Authenticator. It should be unpredictable and unique over the lifetime of a secret, so that an attacker cannot replay an old response.

In a reply it is the Response Authenticator, an MD5 hash proving the answer came from a server that knows the secret. The RFC writes it as MD5(Code+ID+Length+RequestAuth+Attributes+Secret), where + means concatenation.

The User-Password attribute is hidden, not sent in the clear. The password is padded with nulls to a multiple of 16 octets. Then b1 = MD5(S + RA) and c(1) = p1 xor b1, where S is the shared secret and RA the Request Authenticator. Each next block uses bi = MD5(S + c(i-1)) and c(i) = pi xor bi. The result is 16 to 128 octets long.

The shared secret MUST NOT be empty, and the RFC prefers at least 16 octets. Only the password is hidden; other attributes such as User-Name travel unprotected.
sections.eli5: The password is mixed with a secret number that only the guard and the office know, so anyone listening only sees scrambled gibberish. The office's answer carries a signature made the same way.

sections.title: Attributes and Services
sections.content:
Attributes carry everything beyond the basics. The RFC defines types 1 to 63 (with 17 and 21 unassigned and 40 to 59 reserved for accounting). Common ones in a request are User-Name (1), User-Password (2), CHAP-Password (3), NAS-IP-Address (4) and NAS-Port (5). An Access-Request must contain a NAS-IP-Address or a NAS-Identifier, and either a User-Password, a CHAP-Password or a State. It must not contain both a User-Password and a CHAP-Password.

In an Access-Accept, Service-Type (6) says what service the user gets, for example Login or Framed. Framed-Protocol (7), Framed-IP-Address (8), Framed-MTU (12) and the filter and routing attributes set up PPP or SLIP sessions. Reply-Message (18) carries text for the user.

Vendor-Specific (26) lets vendors define their own attributes without changing the protocol. The Vendor-Id is four octets, with a zero high octet and the vendor's SMI Private Enterprise Code in the low three. Servers that do not understand the contents must ignore them.

An attribute table in the RFC says which packet types may carry each attribute and how many times.
sections.eli5: Attributes are labelled notes clipped to a message: "name: nemo", "you may use the phone room", or "this visitor gets 30 minutes". New kinds of notes can be added without confusing old guards.

sections.title: Proxy and Why UDP
sections.content:
With proxy RADIUS, one server receives a request, forwards it to a remote server, and sends the remote server's reply back to the client, possibly changed to reflect local policy. The RFC says a common use is roaming, where two organisations let each other's users dial in. The forwarding server is chosen by the authentication realm, for example the realm part of a Network Access Identifier. The forwarding server decrypts the password with the secret it shares with the client and re-encrypts it with the secret it shares with the remote server. It may add one Proxy-State attribute and must remove it from the reply. Because the reply is signed over the whole packet, the proxy must re-sign it for the client.

Section 2.4 explains why RADIUS uses UDP instead of TCP: retransmission timers are still needed above the transport anyway, a user will not wait minutes for TCP to deliver late data, the protocol is stateless so UDP survives reboots without special handling, and UDP made multi-threaded servers simple. Retransmissions to the same server with unchanged attributes MUST reuse the same Request Authenticator, ID and source port.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the office does not know the visitor, so it phones another company's office and passes the answer back. And the messages are short postcards rather than long phone calls, because a lost postcard is easy to just send again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says security issues are "the primary topic of this document". It advises that each user name be tied to exactly one authentication method, so an attacker cannot negotiate the weakest one from a set. If a user needs different methods in different situations, use distinct user names.

Secrets should be stored so that access is as limited as possible, and distributed through a mechanism that limits how many entities learn them. Secrets must be unguessable; the RFC wants them at least as strong as a well-chosen password, preferably 16 octets or more.

The RFC itself notes that the User-Password hiding method "has not been subjected to significant amounts of cryptanalysis" and some in the IETF worry it may not give enough confidentiality. It tells users to evaluate their threat environment and consider additional mechanisms.

Later RFCs examine these concerns in more depth. RFC 5080 collects implementation issues and fixes. The packet-level design (MD5, no encryption of most attributes) is why modern deployments often tunnel RADIUS inside IPsec or TLS.
sections.eli5: The scramble works, but nobody has studied it very hard, so the rule book tells you to keep your secret long, keep it private, and think about adding a stronger lock.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Packet type. 1 Access-Request, 2 Access-Accept, 3 Access-Reject, 4 Accounting-Request, 5 Accounting-Response, 11 Access-Challenge.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Matches replies to requests. Changes when the attributes change; stays the same on retransmission.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole packet. Minimum 20, maximum 4096.

fields.name: Authenticator
fields.desc: 16 octets. A random Request Authenticator in requests; a Response Authenticator (an MD5 hash) in replies.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Which attribute this is, for example 1 User-Name, 2 User-Password, 26 Vendor-Specific.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole attribute, including Type and Length.

fields.name: Value (first bytes)
fields.desc: Zero or more octets. Format depends on Type: text, string, address, integer or time. Continues past this row.

viz.caption: Two uses of a shared secret

items.title: Hiding the password
items.text: b1 = MD5(secret + Request Authenticator), then the first 16 password octets are XORed with b1. Later blocks chain from the previous ciphertext.

items.title: Signing the reply
items.text: Response Authenticator = MD5 over Code, ID, Length, the Request Authenticator, the reply attributes and then the secret.

items.title: Choosing the secret
items.text: By source IP address of the packet. Never empty; at least 16 octets preferred.

items.title: Freshness
items.text: The Request Authenticator should be unpredictable and unique over a secret's lifetime to stop replay.
